newsitem.title: USA: Russians abort mid-winter McKinley expedition.
newsitem.headline: Russians abort mid-winter McKinley expedition.

text.p: A pair of Russian mountaineers who tried to become the first to reach Mount McKinley's summit in early winter ended their expedition on Monday after one fell into a crevasse on the peak, a National Park Service spokesmen said.

Artur Testov, 31, and Andrey Isupov, 32, both experienced climbers from Moscow, were shuttled on Monday afternoon by air-taxi from McKinley to Talkeetna, the tiny town near the base of North America's tallest mountain.

Testov, the trip leader, fell into a crevasse about 12,500 feet (3,800 metres) up the 20,320-foot (6,194-metre) peak, said Daryl Miller, a Talkeetna-based mountaineering ranger for Denali National Park. In the fall, the climbers lost a sled they were using to tow equipment, Miller said.
Despite the bitterly cold temperatures and high winds on the peak, the Russians appeared in good shape, he added.

Winter expeditions on McKinley are rare. Most climbers ascend the peak between April and July, when daylight is long and weather often calm. The few who try winter expeditions usually pick late February and March, as daylight increases at McKinley's far-north latitude.

The Russians -- who have extensive experience in the Himalayas and the Caucasus -- might have made McKinley history if not for their mishap, said Cliff Hudson, owner of the air-taxi company that flew them to and from the peak's 7,000-foot (2,100-metre) base camp.
"These are good strong people, and they would have probably made it if they hadn't lost their sled down a crevasse," Hudson said.
